query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Thermal stress-induced atom migration is the primary mechanism governing the growth of high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanopillars, with surface diffusion playing a secondary role.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrCuFeNi HEA thin films with a thickness of ∼1 μm, synthesized on (1 0 0)-Si substrates by magnetron sputtering
generation.intervention: Heating and cooling treatment to induce thermal stress on the deposited films
generation.conditions: Heating temperature of 800 °C for 2 h, followed by cooling in a glass tube with argon gas flow
generation.structural_mediator: Thermal stress, surface diffusion, and grain boundary structure
generation.mechanism: Thermal stress-induced atom migration and surface diffusion
generation.predicted_outcome: Growth of HEA nanopillars with a length of ∼600 nm and a diameter of ∼300 nm, with a convex protrusion and roughness of ∼1.5 μm
generation.baseline: No HEA nanopillar growth without thermal stress induction
generation.boundary: Heating temperature range of 700-800 °C, cooling speed, and composition of the HEA
generation.uncertainty: Role of surface diffusion in the growth mechanism, optimal temperature for other HEA compositions, and effect of grain boundary structure on nanopillar growth

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of HEA nanopillar growth with and without thermal stress induction, using varying heating temperatures and cooling speeds
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: No HEA nanopillar growth observed with thermal stress induction, or significant difference in nanopillar morphology and size with varying heating temperatures and cooling speeds

Compared with bulk counterparts, nanostructured HEA materials could be even more fascinating in terms of further enhanced mechanical performance, enhanced damage tolerance and other superior properties that bulk counterparts do not possess. To our knowledge, at least three types of nanostructures, namely, HEA nanopillars, nanoporous HEA and HEA nanoparticles have been successfully fabricated. NbMoTaW HEA nanopillars were successfully fabricated by using focused ion beams (FIB) to mill small-scale pillars (SPs). Due to the well-known size effect in nanomaterials, as predicted, such HEA pillar showed much higher yield strength than that of its bulk form. A method for making HEA nanoparticles with up to eight different elements has been developed, which relied on shocking metal salt-covered carbon nanofibers and followed by rapid quenching. It could therefore be a promising low-cost approach to fabricating HEA SPs.
As noted in the review article written by the co-founder of HEAs, computational works are significantly lacking in the design and development of HEAs. According to the review paper, more than 30 metal elements had been successfully mixed to produce over 300 HEA combinations alone. Since each combination allows different composing concentrations, the acute possible HEAs are uncountable. Surface morphologies show the convex protrusion with the width in an interval of ∼5 μm and roughness of ∼1.5 μm, in which the CoCrCuFeNi HEA SPs were revealed. The roughness measurement by atomic force microscopy (AFM) in Fig. 2(g) depicts the deepness between convex and concave. Fig. 2(e and f) show the elemental state of Cu and Fe. The convex and concave zones in Fig. 2(c and d) can be thought of as splits between the Cu-rich/Fe-lean zone and Cu-lean/Fe-rich zone by thermal stress-induced elemental rearrangement. It means that the CoCrCuFeNi HEA SPs tend to grow in Cu-rich/Fe-lean zones. In Fig. 2(h), different elemental distribution was plotted. The proportion of Co, Cr, and Ni was almost equivalent in at%, whereas that of Cu and Fe was significantly different as shown in Fig. 2(e and f).
